text: The scenario: the Service Desk wants a My Open Requests widget for the portal Homepage. A caller should see their own Requested Items, most recent first, each as a card with a colored left border matching its state, and a View Details button. We'll build all four parts in order: Server Script, HTML Template, CSS, then Client Controller.

The Server Script queries sc_req_item, filtering on request dot requested_for using gs dot getUserID. That's a dot-walk — sc_req_item doesn't store a requester directly, so the query reaches through the parent Request record to find who actually asked for it. The script also computes a state_class right here, server-side, translating the raw numeric state into a CSS class name, instead of pushing that raw number to the client.

The HTML Template loops with ng-repeat over c dot data dot items, rendering one request-card per item. The key line is class equals request-card, then item dot state_class interpolated straight into that class attribute — that's what connects the server-computed class name to an actual rendered class on the page.

The CSS defines four border-left colors, one per state class: blue for open, amber for work in progress, green for complete. Because the HTML Template already renders the right class name on each card, the correct color just appears — no client-side JavaScript has to decide it.

The Client Controller defines c dot viewDetails, called by the template's ng-click on the View Details button. It hands spNavigator the item's sys_id and its table name, sc_req_item, so it opens that specific Requested Item's own detail page inside the portal.

That's the same four-way split every Service Portal widget uses: the Server Script decides what data exists, the HTML and CSS decide how it's structured and colored, and the Client Controller decides what happens on a click. Simple or complex, every widget breaks down exactly this way.

With Service Portal widgets built end to end, Chapter 7 is complete.
